problem: how to use histogram, set exposure lightroom, avoid blown highlights, whites blacks clipping

technique: Histogram-driven exposure with Alt-drag white/black points
exact_steps: Trust histogram, not screen. Histogram = pixel brightness graph: far left pure black (no detail), center midtones (skin lives here), far right pure white (blown). Set Exposure first: push until skin midtones read correctly without graph slamming the right wall. Contrast slider 10-20 only for portraits (more crushes shadows/blows highlights; use tone curve for heavier contrast). Set true black: hold Alt/Option dragging Blacks left until pixels appear. Use clipping warnings to stop just before specular red (highlight) or blue (shadow) clip indicators show.

problem: sora 2 prompt structure, director level sora prompt, cinematic ai ad prompt, time coded shotlist
symptom: Sora 2 invents details you didn't want, weak lip-sync, inconsistent space across cuts
technique: Sora 2 long-prompt: Production Brief vs Time-Coded Shotlist
exact_steps: Sora 2 is a reasoning model: anything you don't specify it invents. Choose length by intent: short prompt = declare format+style upfront and let it interpret; long prompt = director control. PRODUCTION BRIEF (atmospheric single scene) blocks: Format & tone; Main subject(s); Wardrobe and props; Location & framing (anchor foreground/mid/background for spatial continuity); Lighting & palette; Continuity rules (weather/time-of-day held across cuts); Actions & camera beats (1-3 timed beats, each pairs ONE camera move + ONE subject action); Montage plan (cuts, inserts, transitions, pacing like 'three fast inserts then 0.5s hold'); Dialogue (own labeled block for accurate lip-sync); Sound & foley (micro-sounds: peel, snap, pour); Finish (film grain, halation, LUT intent, poster frame). TIME-CODED SHOTLIST (fast ads): Header 'An [N]-second [FORMAT] with [TRANSITIONS] and [CAMERA STYLE]' then bracketed beats [0-A s] OPEN, [A-B] TRANSITION, etc., each = SHOT SIZE+ANGLE + ACTION + CAMERA BEHAVIOR + CUT/TRANSITION + AUDIO. Duration guide: 4s about 2-3 beats, 8s about 5 beats, 12s about 6-7 beats. Safety: no realistic real-person faces in image-to-video (use stylized), no celebrity-lookalike wording, no protected IP.

problem: blurry background portrait, depth of field, bokeh, make photo look professional, separate subject from background
symptom: Portraits look flat and amateur because the background is sharp and competes with the subject's face.
technique: Aperture-priority + max zoom for shallow DOF (the pro look)
exact_steps: 1) Put the camera in Aperture Priority mode. 2) Dial the f-stop to the SMALLEST number your lens allows (f/2.8, or f/3.5 if that is the lowest). 3) Zoom the lens to its MAXIMUM zoom / longest focal length. 4) Focus on the subject's face. Result: face is tack sharp, background is fully blown out and blurry. Phone equivalent: use the camera app's Portrait mode. The two levers that create the blur are the widest aperture plus the longest focal length, focused on the eyes.
inputs_needed: A camera with aperture priority (or phone with Portrait mode), a subject, a background with depth behind them
output_artifact: A portrait with a tack-sharp face and a fully defocused background
when_to_use: Any single-subject portrait where you want pro subject-background separation (Reset headshots, IG hero, dating/LinkedIn profile shots).
when_not: Group photos or environmental/scenic shots where you need front-to-back sharpness; very tight spaces where you cannot zoom in.

problem: make body part look bigger or smaller, hide stomach in photo, slim waist with pose, what to push toward camera
symptom: Whatever is closest to the lens looks enlarged, so flat-on stances make hips/waist/midsection look heavy and shrink the face.
technique: Proximity rule: closest to lens = largest (push assets forward, push flaws back)
exact_steps: Core rule: the thing closest to the camera receives the most spotlight and looks LARGER; the thing farther away looks smaller. To slim the lower body: shift weight to the BACK leg so hips/waist kick AWAY from camera, then lean the chest TOWARD camera. The same subject can look ~half as wide hips-to-hips just by kicking hips back vs forward, with no change to lens or angle. To enlarge eyes in a headshot: have subject lean in and look up, or raise the camera angle so the eyes sit closer to the lens than the body. To show off a worked-out arm: bring it to the front / lean on it. Hand test to prove it: a hand by the face looks normal; pushed toward the lens it looks bigger than the face; pulled back it looks tiny.
inputs_needed: Subject, ability to direct weight shift and camera height
output_artifact: A flattering frame where the desired feature is emphasized and the unflattering area is minimized
when_to_use: Every portrait. First lever to reach for when a body area reads too heavy or a feature reads too small.
when_not: When you deliberately want a documentary/honest representation and not optical flattery.

problem: pose women, S curve, contrapposto, make pose feminine, flatter female form, thin the legs
symptom: Square, feet-wide, symmetrical stances look cheery and childish, not elegant; everything reads wide.
technique: Build the S-curve (contrapposto) from the feet up
exact_steps: 1) Square the subject up, put ankles together. 2) Lift one heel (just the heel) to start thinning. 3) Collapse/bend that same knee inward, which thins that whole section and bends the straight line into an S. 4) Turn that hip subtly AWAY from camera to thin further. 5) Shift weight onto the back hip. The painting term is contrapposto: a slight S-curve through the body is what flatters most people. Rule of thumb for women full-length: if you can bend it, bend it; if you can curve it, curve it. To deepen: front leg forward and up on toe, then arch the lower back (cue 'stick your butt out' not 'stick your stomach out') to reveal the lower-back curve.
inputs_needed: Subject who can stand and shift weight; sometimes an apple box for the front foot
output_artifact: An elegant, curvy standing pose with weight shift and visible S-line
when_to_use: Standing female portraits (Reset, editorial), brides, seniors where elegance is the goal.
when_not: Masculine male posing (use the V instead); fully symmetrical/regimental looks done on purpose.

problem: pose men, make man look masculine, broad shoulders, posing tips for men, avoid feminine pose
symptom: Men stand straight, flat-footed, hands over crotch with feet parted; the form reads boxy with no peaks and valleys (like the letter I).
technique: Create the masculine V and turn the body toward the light
exact_steps: 1) Posing starts from the feet: shake them out, bring feet together, then bend the knee CLOSEST to the camera and put all weight on the BACK leg. 2) Hang the body forward in a 'glorified slouch' and lean the chest toward camera, creating peaks and valleys (a V, not an I). 3) Turn the whole body TOWARD the light source (cue: 'pretend you're on a turntable, your feet and legs turn too') to make him look bigger and broader. 4) Give the hands a job: one or both hands in pockets (thumbs IN or fully out, never four fingers out, never frame the crotch). 5) Bring elbows out slightly for a gap/silhouette. Note: turning a man AWAY from the light (the female recipe) reads feminine and thin, so avoid unless intended.
inputs_needed: Subject, an identifiable directional light source (window, garage door, key light)
output_artifact: A masculine standing portrait with V-shape, broad chest/shoulders, and relaxed slouch
when_to_use: Male standing portraits, business/brand headshots for men, plus-size men (lean further forward + chin out).
when_not: Female posing (turn away from light instead); when an intentionally androgynous/feminine look is wanted.

problem: run out of poses, how to never run out of poses, systematic posing, change pose quickly, posing framework
symptom: Photographer or subject freezes and repeats the same 2-3 poses; thinks a new pose must be a drastically different shape.
technique: Seven posing points + rotate-for-a-new-pose (Sue Bryce system)
exact_steps: Work bottom-up through the seven joints/zones: 1) FEET/ankles: feet together to shoulder-width to wider; and rotate the whole body a little (a tiny rotation = a brand-new pose). 2) KNEES: tippy-toe one foot to activate the knee, bring it in (smaller/daintier) or out (wider/bolder). 3) HIP: shift weight/balance onto one leg (like waiting for a bus) and kick the hip out (straight stick becomes an avocado curve). 4) SHOULDERS: forward (vulnerable), back (strong), or one down toward the chin (sassy). 5) ELBOWS/wrists: hand shapes (intermediate). 6) HANDS: if stuck, do what you do daily (fix glasses, jeans, hair). 7) HEAD/NECK: tilts and chin-around; even a small chin move is a new pose. Change the legs first, the nose/chin last. The big takeaway: when you run out, just rotate slightly.
inputs_needed: Subject, awareness of the seven zones
output_artifact: An expanded set of distinct frames generated by adjusting one joint at a time
when_to_use: Any session where you or the subject runs dry; training a non-model; pacing a high-volume shoot.
when_not: n/a (universal scaffolding); skip the verbal labels if they make the subject overthink.

problem: subject looks stiff, awkward poses, get natural expressions, model frozen, break set selfie poses
symptom: Non-models lock into stiff, repeated 'set' poses (head tilt, peace sign) and look frozen; static frames feel lifeless.
technique: Movement + burst + isolated micro-motions to get natural shapes and real expressions
exact_steps: 1) Raise frames-per-second to ~5-10 fps (burst). 2) Get the subject MOVING: walking, skipping, jumping, spinning, swaying side to side, rocking on heels. Build up walking to skipping to jumping. 3) Fire the burst as they shift weight onto the FRONT foot (that frame captures the movement). 4) Catch the real expression AFTER the motion (everyone laughs after skipping). For a controlled version, give ONE isolated micro-motion at a time then reset (face this corner and rotate to me; take a step back and walk through the mark). For the fake-walking pose: give a floor mark, keep stride wide, and have them look back as if their name was called. Movement also breaks ingrained selfie habits.

output_artifact: A run of candid, dynamic frames with natural body language and genuine expression

problem: what to do with hands, awkward hands in photos, posing arms, thin the arms, hands look big
symptom: Subjects do not know what to do with their hands; arms pressed to the body look heavy; hands point at the crotch or look claw-like.
technique: Hand and arm placement: pockets, gaps, pull-back, soft fingers
exact_steps: Hands: give them a job. Pockets are the safety net: thumb in / hand halfway / fully in. For men in jeans use thumb-in; in dress pants the whole hand goes in; if the thumb is out, point it DOWN, never horizontal. Avoid four fingers out and avoid framing the crotch. Arms: keep them OFF the body (pressing creates mass) by creating a GAP between arm and torso so the waist shape reads; this also makes a flattering triangle of negative space. To slim a heavier arm, pull the elbow BACK behind the hip line so the back half hides and recedes. Do not press the arm against the body in profile; float the elbow slightly forward so the arm looks slimmer. Fingers: keep them soft and relaxed, slight bend in the elbow (no toy-soldier straight arms); show both hands (a hidden hand looks like a missing limb); offer one or several fingers loosely, wrists relaxed.

output_artifact: Natural, relaxed hand/arm placement with slimming gaps and soft fingers

problem: arm looks like a nub, legs look short, foreshortening, flat feet boring pose, static rigid pose
symptom: Limbs aimed at the lens compress into stubs; flat-footed locked-knee stances look static and push the stomach forward; symmetrical pairs read rigid.
technique: Posing checklist: kill foreshortening, kill flat feet, stagger the levels
exact_steps: Run a mental checklist on every frame: 1) FORESHORTENING: any limb coming straight to/from the lens compresses and loses context (elbow toward camera = arm becomes a nub; knees/feet at camera in a seated shot = smooshed legs; fingers pointing at lens on a table). Fix by lowering the arm to the side, turning knees/feet to the side, or angling the appendage across the frame. 2) FLAT FEET: never both feet flat with knees locked (it pushes the stomach forward and is static). Get feet on different levels (bend a knee, toe up, apple box, a step) to introduce a curve and shift hips back/chest forward. 3) LEVELS: when there are two of anything (feet, knees, hands, elbows, shoulders), do NOT keep them even or doing the same thing; stagger them to make the pose dynamic. Also watch for MERGERS: check the silhouette has negative space so the body does not read as a blob.
inputs_needed: Subject; optional apple boxes/steps for level changes
output_artifact: A dynamic, elongated full-length pose free of compressed limbs and rigid symmetry
when_to_use: Full-length and seated portraits; any pose that feels boxy, short, or static.
when_not: When deliberate symmetry/foreshortening is the creative intent.

problem: subject looks wide, full width experienced, turn body to slim, negative space, triangles in pose
symptom: Anything square to the camera is experienced at full width; subjects who do not want their full width seen still stand front-on.
technique: Put the body on an axis + add negative space and triangles
exact_steps: Anything square to the lens reads at its full width, so put the body on an AXIS: rotate to a diagonal, put weight on the back hip, rotate the front foot out, hands in pockets for a lean, relaxed line. Pose bottom-up (set body language first, then the face). Counterbalance width with NEGATIVE SPACE: when the viewer sees the boundary/gap, they read where the shape ends, so create gaps between arm and torso. Triangles are the most aesthetically appealing negative-space shape, so build triangles with the limbs. If a loose garment fills the gap, clamp it behind to restore the negative space. Anti-sink cue when they slump on the axis: 'pull up through the base of the spine, drop the shoulders, weight in the back hip.' Tighten the abdominal wall (feeling of a crunch), never 'suck in your stomach.'

problem: short light vs broad light, make face look thinner or wider, light direction for posing, sculpt face with light
symptom: Subject turned the wrong way relative to the light looks flat, too wide, or too thin for their face/gender goal.
technique: Turn the face into short light (slim) or broad light (wider/masculine)
exact_steps: Identify where the light comes from FIRST. SHORT LIGHT: subject faces toward the light so the lit side of the face is the NARROWER side away from camera; this slims the face (good for women, thin/heavier subjects you want narrowed). BROAD LIGHT: turn so the broader, camera-side of the face is lit; this enlarges the face and reads more masculine (good for a thin man you want broader; risky for a large face/large guy whose head can then look gigantic). Match light direction to the posing goal: turning a man toward the light broadens him (masculine V); turning a woman away from the light slims her. Same logic sculpts dimension: side light shades one side of the face to create the 2D-to-3D shaded-apple effect.

output_artifact: A portrait where light direction reinforces the desired face width and dimension

problem: subject can't take direction, freeze up posing, give model a reference, relax client, mirror posing
symptom: Telling a subject 'left/right' confuses them; direct verbal posing makes them stiff and self-conscious.
technique: Show-don't-tell + mirroring + the relax-and-catch reset
exact_steps: 1) MIRROR: instead of saying turn left/right, demo the pose and have them copy you as if looking in a mirror (attach a bit of humor to disarm them). 2) SHOW-DON'T-TELL with references: pull portraits (Pinterest, Annie Leibovitz, Mark Seliger, movie posters) on a phone/iPad, say 'this is the kind of thing I'm thinking,' even set it on the floor in front of them; they mimic it, then naturally adjust into a better, more genuine pose. 3) RELAX-AND-CATCH: when out of ideas, say 'just relax a minute, I'm changing camera settings' (you are not), keep one eye on them, and when they slip into their natural posture say 'hold that' and shoot (works only once or twice per shoot). 4) Pre-shoot warm-up: run through the poses, read their shyness/outgoingness, and use mirroring so they learn to take instruction. 5) Slow down, chat, observe; the natural moments happen when you stop firing. 6) Do NOT manhandle the client; mirror and cue ('put your hand here') instead of physically moving them, and ask first if you must.
inputs_needed: Reference images on a phone/iPad; a tripod helps so you can shoot without recomposing; rapport
output_artifact: Relaxed, genuine frames from a subject who could not take abstract verbal direction

when_not: Experienced models who pose better with freedom (let them freestyle instead).

problem: lens choice for groups, wide angle distorts faces, compression, focal length for family photos, heads small on ends
symptom: Wide lenses up close distort people on the ends (small heads, stretched features); shooting too close to any face distorts it.
technique: Back up and compress: long lens for groups and flattering portraits
exact_steps: For groups/families, back UP and shoot long (85mm, 100mm, up to 200mm) to compress the subjects and background; do not grab a wide lens just to fit everyone in. At 35mm or wider the people on the ends distort and their heads shrink on the sensor (use ~17-20mm only when you intentionally want to show the whole place as an art print, accepting tiny heads). For individuals: situate the camera FARTHER away and zoom in rather than getting close, because the lens distorts everything up close; keep the camera level and around shoulder height; avoid heavy tilt. Prime-lens discipline: know your focal lengths (e.g. 35 and 50) so you enter a session already knowing the shots each lens will give. iPhone fix for a bad angle after the fact: crop tool to Distortion modes to change the apparent shooting angle.
inputs_needed: A longer lens or zoom, room to step back, group or single subject
output_artifact: Group and portrait frames with natural proportions and compressed, flattering perspective

when_not: Tight rooms with no room to retreat; when an exaggerated wide environmental/fisheye look is the goal.

problem: pose couples, couple kiss looks awkward, wedding couple poses, posing two people, variations couples
symptom: When told to 'kiss,' couples go nose-to-nose and pucker, which flattens both faces; couple poses feel repetitive.
technique: Almost-kiss + LASH variations for couples
exact_steps: ALMOST KISS: turn the person whose hair/makeup you want shown toward the camera and the other away; have them tilt heads, bring faces close, and SMILE close-up (it feels awkward but reads pretty), then let them actually kiss afterward without smudged noses. For same-sex couples, switch who turns which way between frames. LASH = the four variations you can run inside any couple pose (except back-to-back): L = Laugh (cue them to look at each other and laugh normally), A = Almost kiss, S = Smile (one at the other / one at camera, or a slay/look-off), H = Heads (foreheads together, head on shoulder, kiss the cheek). Lock the base pose and tell the couple to HOLD it (re-setting wastes seconds); unbutton a man's jacket button for arm poses (and only ever button the top button of a blazer).

problem: portrait lighting patterns, where to place the light, rembrandt loop split butterfly broad short
symptom: User doesn't know where to position a single light relative to the face to get a named, intentional look
technique: Nine-pattern clock placement system
exact_steps: Imagine a clock with the camera at 6 o'clock facing 12 and the subject in the center; place the light (flash or sun) at a clock hour. SPLIT: light at 9 or 3 (one side lit, one side shadow; harsh, shows wrinkles). BACKLIGHT/RIM: light at 12 behind subject. BUTTERFLY: light at 6, slightly above and in front (shadow under nose). CLAMSHELL: butterfly plus a reflector or fill light directly underneath. LOOP: main light just above eye level at 5 or 7 o'clock (small nose shadow, flatters most). REMBRANDT: light at 4 or 8 o'clock, far enough that the nose shadow joins the cheek shadow, leaving an upside-down triangle of light under the opposite eye. problem: understand light quality strength direction, hard vs soft, front side back light
symptom: User can't reason about why a scene looks the way it does or how to change it without gear
technique: Three core light concepts + three shooting directions
exact_steps: Evaluate every light source on three axes: QUALITY (natural/sun is highest quality and gets soft; many artificial sources are low quality, e.g. flickering coffee-shop bulbs, and never fully mimic the sun); STRENGTH (strong source = hard, contrasty; weak source = soft, lower contrast; cameras capture ~13-15 stops of dynamic range vs the eye's ~21-24, so harsh light forces you to choose highlights or shadows); DIRECTION (the biggest lever). Then pick a direction: FRONT light (light behind you) = even exposure but flat, few shadows; SIDE light = beautiful shadows, depth, the default to reach for; BACK light = deepest/darkest shadows and drama, risks silhouette if too strong. Shift your own perspective relative to subject and source to change direction without moving lights. Modify with a softbox (artificial) or 5-in-1 reflector (reflect or diffuse through a white sheet); use smoke/haze/mist for atmospheric rays; white surfaces bounce soft light, black cards/walls absorb to deepen shadows.

problem: best time of day to shoot, golden hour blue hour midday overcast, natural light planning

technique: Four natural-light windows + shoot-into-shadows discipline
exact_steps: GOLDEN HOUR (sunrise/sunset): soft directional side light, low contrast, easiest for the sensor; note sunrise vs sunset put the sun in different parts of the sky, so a scene backlit at sunrise may be front-lit at sunset (use Photo Pills to predict the sun's position). BLUE HOUR (~1 hr before sunrise / after sunset): very soft with a blue tint, dreamy/moody, but dark, so open up the aperture (e.g. f/1.4). MIDDAY/HARD LIGHT: fine for cities (tall buildings cut hard light into geometric lines, leading lines, deep shadows); bad for foliage/nature (hot spots on leaves); wait ~2 hours off noon for softer angles. OVERCAST: clouds diffuse the sun into soft even light, great for portraits and even face exposure. Core discipline: you can't change light after capture, so get it right in camera; SHOOT INTO THE SHADOWS (side/back light) instead of front light for depth; treat light itself as a possible subject; shift perspective to rescue bad light.

problem: hard vs soft light control, inverse square law falloff, why far light still soft in small room
symptom: User can't predict shadow hardness/falloff or why a distant light looks low-contrast indoors
technique: Apparent-size hard/soft control + inverse square law
exact_steps: Hardness depends on the light's APPARENT SIZE from the subject's view: a large source close = soft, big, low-texture; a small source (or any source far away, since distance shrinks apparent size) = hard, more texture, harsher specular highlights. Closer light = bigger = softer; further = smaller = harder. INVERSE SQUARE LAW: light falls off faster the closer it is to the subject (quick intensity drop over a given distance) and more gradually when far. Counterintuitive trap: in a confined/small studio a far light should be harder, but more of its light bounces off walls and fills the shadows, so the image actually reads LOWER contrast. To raise contrast in a small space, flag the bounce with black polys/cards; to soften, enlarge the source or bring it closer. Also control: position (front = less shadow/texture; side/low = more; below = unsettling/horror feel) and color (kelvin/white balance, full vs low spectrum). Modifiers must be used at appropriate distance, not too far.
inputs_needed: A controllable light, modifiers, black flags, knowledge of room size
output_artifact: Predictable shadow hardness and contrast control
when_to_use: Diagnosing or designing contrast and falloff, especially in small spaces
when_not: When you simply want to follow a fixed recipe without tuning falloff

problem: reusable Photoshop moodboard template, grid moodboard fast, quick printable shoot board
symptom: Photoshop grid does not match the ruler; images do not snap cleanly; rebuilding the layout every time is slow
technique: Reusable A4 percentage-grid template + masked-box collage in Photoshop
exact_steps: 1) File > New > document type International Paper (A4). 2) View > Rulers and View > Show > Grid. 3) Right-click ruler > set to Percent. 4) Edit > Preferences > Guides, Grid & Slices: set gridline every 10 with 4 subdivisions (line every 2.5%) so grid matches the percentage ruler. 5) View > Snap and Snap To > Grid + Guides on. (Snap may only catch vertical lines; pull horizontal guides from the top ruler at 10%, 20%, etc., grabbing with the Move tool.) 6) Draw boxes: rectangle + new layer + paint bucket; duplicate (Cmd/Ctrl+J), move, Free Transform (Cmd/Ctrl+T) into varied sizes leaving 1-cell gaps. 7) Merge all box layers (select top, shift+select bottom, Ctrl/Cmd+E). 8) Ctrl/Cmd-click the merged layer to load selection, new layer, Select > Inverse, fill the surround gray (later white) = the mask/template. problem: expose for skin tone, darker skin underexposed, blown highlights light skin, meter the face, spot metering portrait
symptom: darker skin fades into background, lighter skin blows out on forehead/nose, camera averages the exposure wrong
technique: Meter for the Face (Skin-Tone Exposure Discipline)
exact_steps: Spot meter on the FACE, not the averaged frame. Darker skin tones: find the light, commit to the exposure, do not underexpose to protect other highlights; meter for the face and add +2/3 to +1 full stop of exposure compensation (the in-camera meter underexposes darker skin). Lighter skin tones: meter for the highlights, pull down or diffuse the key, subtract -2/3 to -1 stop so skin texture holds at the cost of a slightly darker shadow side. For a subject backlit by bright sky (camera silhouettes them): add light to the face (flash/reflector/closer brighter key) OR move the subject so light is on the face. Protect the face; let other highlights resolve in post.

Zoom to the LONGER end of your lens (longer focal length compresses and blurs the background further). Focus on the eyes, specifically the NEAR eye (not the bridge of the nose, not the cheek). On a phone, use Portrait mode. These four steps produce the professional blurred-background look before any other decision matters.

problem: where to place subject on location, on-location workflow order, chasing light and background problems
symptom: constantly fighting light and background issues that the pose cannot fix, posing before checking light
technique: Light / Location / Layout Sequence
exact_steps: Run this strict 3-step sequence on every new spot within a location. 1) LIGHT first: find where the sun is, where your shadow is, where bounce/fill comes from; place the subject so light lands on the face without being blown out or lost in shadow. 2) LOCATION second: check the background behind the subject for dark holes, busy distractions, or clipping elements behind the head; adjust your angle or the subject's position until the background is clean. 3) LAYOUT last: only now pose the subject, using the composition and lighting to advantage instead of fighting them. Never start with layout, that forces you to chase light/background problems the pose cannot fix.
inputs_needed: Location, subject, awareness of sun/shadow/bounce surfaces
output_artifact: A frame where light, background, and pose all serve the image (in that priority)
when_to_use: Every new spot on every location shoot
when_not: Fully pre-lit studio where light and background are already locked

problem: how to pose a subject, generate poses fast, run out of poses, posing vocabulary, male and female default pose
symptom: subject poses stiff/awkward, photographer freezes on what to pose next, men cross hands over crotch, women stand square and stiff
technique: Seven Posing Points + Male/Female Defaults + Rotation Trick
exact_steps: Treat a pose as 7 independent levers; adjust ONE at a time, leave the other six, the pose changes each time (cycle all seven in a 2-minute session for ~20 frames). 1) Feet: planted wide/together/tiptoe, rotated in/out. 2) Knee: bending the FRONT knee is the most reliable small-change move. 3) Hip: shift weight onto one leg for the natural waiting-for-a-bus stance. 4) Torso: slight forward lean (glorified slouch) brings chest/shoulders forward, pushes gut away. 5) Shoulders: square=confrontational, angled=at ease, turned=profile/elegant. 6) Arms/hands: men=hands in pockets (thumbs IN, fingers outside the pant); women=one hand at collar/waist/hair. 7) Head/eyes: chin slightly down and forward to reduce double chin, nose toward the light, eyes to lens for connection or past it for mood. MALE recovery: turn whole body toward the light, hands in pockets (thumbs in), feet close, bend front knee, slight forward lean, chin forward+down. FEMALE recovery: shift weight to one leg, resting leg on tiptoe/bent, one hand to a body point, angle shoulders off square, chin down + nose to light, commit the eyes. ROTATION TRICK: when out of poses, rotate the subject; 45 deg = a new pose, 90 deg = another, back-to-camera with torso twisted = another.
inputs_needed: Subject in frame, a light source to turn toward
output_artifact: A repeatable pose vocabulary generating many usable frames from one starting pose
when_to_use: Every portrait session; especially untrained subjects and when poses run dry
when_not: Fast candid/documentary capture where directing would break the moment

problem: how to build a moodboard, moodboard structure for a shoot, pinterest graveyard, brief the team and client
symptom: team shows up in different aesthetic directions, board is 30 disagreeing images, client unsure photographer can deliver
technique: Five-Page Moodboard + Working Discipline
exact_steps: Build exactly 3-5 pages (do not skip, do not add more). Page 1 Title image: one hero that makes the client think 'this is the photographer' (single most important page). Page 2 Tone: 3-5 images setting emotional register (warmth/tension/formality/playfulness). Page 3 Hair, makeup, styling: two images per bucket chosen for CONSISTENCY not variety. Page 4 Lighting reference: 3-5 images showing the SAME lighting direction, quality, and contrast (the team's technical brief). Page 5 Location reference: 2-4 images of the space type or the actual scouted location. Discipline: one secret board per project named for the shoot (not a mega-board); remove any image that conflicts with the direction even if you like it; lock the board before outreach. AI diagnostic: drive a reference render with a void prompt (just a pair of quotation marks) to see what the board produces stylistically independent of subject. In Midjourney, control board influence with stylize value (default 100; drop toward 15-50 if output clones the board; up to 1000 forces near-total adherence) and run style raw in parallel as a second draft. Deliver three versions: 3-5pg PDF/link to client; condensed 2-3pg (title/tone/styling/outfit, no lighting brief) to model; full board + call sheet to team, before the shoot with more than one day lead.
inputs_needed: Source images, a layout tool (Milanote), shoot concept; optionally Midjourney for reference renders
output_artifact: A locked 5-page visual brief delivered in client/model/team versions
when_to_use: Before every shoot, before any model/stylist outreach
when_not: Never skip; even a compressed shoot gets a compressed (still 5-page) board
example_command: os_technique_cards solve "build a 5-page moodboard that aligns the team"
